claim: Multidrug ATP binding cassette (ABC) exporters are ubiquitous ABC transporters that extrude cytotoxic molecules across cell membranes.
source: Multidrug ATP binding cassette (ABC) exporters are ubiquitous ABC transporters that extrude cytotoxic molecules across cell membranes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ABC exporters.

claim: BmrCD is a representative of the heterodimer family of ABC exporters that have an intrinsically impaired nucleotide binding site.
source: Here, we have investigated the conformational cycle of BmrCD, a representative of the heterodimer family of ABC exporters that have an intrinsically impaired nucleotide binding site.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of BmrCD.

claim: The results expose previously unobserved structural intermediates of the NBDs arising from asymmetric configuration of catalytically inequivalent nucleotide binding sites.
source: The results expose previously unobserved structural intermediates of the NBDs arising from asymmetric configuration of catalytically inequivalent nucleotide binding sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by DEER spectroscopy data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The two-state transition of the TMD, from an inward- to an outward-facing conformation, is driven exclusively by ATP hydrolysis.
source: The two-state transition of the TMD, from an inward- to an outward-facing conformation, is driven exclusively by ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by distance distribution measurements in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: These findings provide direct evidence of divergence in the mechanism of ABC exporters.
source: These findings provide direct evidence of divergence in the mechanism of ABC exporters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of BmrCD and MsbA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ABC importers drive accumulation of nutrients in the cytoplasm against their concentration gradients.
source: In prokaryotes, ABC importers drive accumulation of nutrients in the cytoplasm against their concentration gradients while ABC exporters remove toxic substrates out of the cytoplasm and may function as flippases of lipids (Higgins and Linton, 2004; Rees et al., 2009; Sharom, 2011; George and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ABC exporters remove toxic substrates out of the cytoplasm and may function as flippases of lipids.
source: In prokaryotes, ABC importers drive accumulation of nutrients in the cytoplasm against their concentration gradients while ABC exporters remove toxic substrates out of the cytoplasm and may function as flippases of lipids (Higgins and Linton, 2004; Rees et al., 2009; Sharom, 2011; George and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian ABC transporters, such as P-glycoprotein (Pgp) and cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), are exclusively of the exporter class.
source: Mammalian ABC transporters, such as P-glycoprotein (Pgp) and cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), are exclusively of the exporter class, play critical physiological roles and are associated with disease (Higgins and Linton, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian ABC transporters play critical physiological roles and are associated with disease.
source: Mammalian ABC transporters, such as P-glycoprotein (Pgp) and cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), are exclusively of the exporter class, play critical physiological roles and are associated with disease (Higgins and Linton, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Importers and exporters share a modular molecular architecture featuring two nucleotide binding domains (NBDs or ATP binding cassettes) that turnover ATP and two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that are presumed to form a translocation pathway across the bilayer.
source: Importers and exporters share a modular molecular architecture featuring two nucleotide binding domains (NBDs or ATP binding cassettes) that turnover ATP and two transmembrane domains (TMDs) that are presumed to form a translocation pathway across the bilayer.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ABC transporter architecture.

claim: The four modules of ABC transporters can be encoded by separate genes and assembled as homo- or hetero-dimers, or expressed as a single polypeptide chain.
source: The four modules of ABC transporters can be encoded by separate genes and assembled as homo- or hetero-dimers, or expressed as a single polypeptide chain (Higgins and Linton, 2004; Rees et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Crystallographic snapshots of ABC importers have revealed inward- and outward-facing states.
source: Crystallographic snapshots of ABC importers have revealed inward- and outward-facing states (Locher et al., 2002; Hollenstein et al., 2007; Oldham et al., 2008; Korkhov et al., 2012) in the nomenclature of Jardetzky's alternating access model (Jardetzky, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: The proposed structural mechanism of ABC exporters invokes two states captured by crystallography: Inward-facing devoid of substrates and/or nucleotides (referred to as apo) and outward-facing with bound nucleotides.
source: In contrast, the proposed structural mechanism of ABC exporters is less elaborate invoking two states captured by crystallography: Inward-facing devoid of substrates and/or nucleotides (referred to as apo) (Ward et al., 2007; Aller et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012) and outward-facing with bound nucleotides (Dawson and Locher, 2006, 2007; Ward et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: There is no consensus regarding the suite of conformational steps that couple ATP hydrolysis to substrate translocation in ABC exporters.
source: While these structures highlight the possible range of conformational motion, there is no consensus regarding the suite of conformational steps that couple ATP hydrolysis to substrate translocation (George and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Inward-facing structures of the bacterial homodimer MsbA and eukaryotic Pgp have inverted V-shapes wherein the two leaflets of the transporters are separated by a large chamber open to the cytoplasm and the bilayer.
source: Inward-facing structures of the bacterial homodimer MsbA (Ward et al., 2007) and eukaryotic Pgp (Aller et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2012) have inverted V-shapes wherein the two leaflets of the transporters are separated by a large chamber open to the cytoplasm and the bilayer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: In nucleotide and substrate-free structures of MsbA and Pgp, the two NBDs are disengaged and separated by 10–50 Å.
source: In these nucleotide and substrate-free structures, the two NBDs are disengaged and separated by 10–50 Å.
evidence: This is a description of structural features from crystal structures cited in the previous sentence.

claim: In nucleotide-bound, outward-facing structures of MsbA and Sav1866, the two NBDs are in close contact, bringing together the ABC signature motif from one subunit and the Walker A and Walker B sequences from the other subunit to form the nucleotide binding sites (NBSs).
source: In contrast, nucleotide-bound, outward-facing structures of MsbA (Ward et al., 2007) and its homolog Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2006, 2007) have the two NBDs in close contact, bringing together the ABC signature motif from one subunit and the Walker A and Walker B sequences from the other subunit to form the nucleotide binding sites (NBSs).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: Central elements of the alternating access model are considered inconsistent with mechanistic studies, primarily of the mammalian ABC exporter Pgp, implying catalytic asymmetry between the two NBSs and constant contact between the NBDs during transport.
source: However, central elements of this model are considered inconsistent with mechanistic studies, primarily of the mammalian ABC exporter Pgp, implying catalytic asymmetry between the two NBSs and constant contact between the NBDs during transport (Tombline and Senior, 2005; Siarheyeva et al., 2010; George and Jones, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: An apo state, devoid of nucleotides, is unlikely to be populated or is transient under cellular ATP concentrations which are typically an order of magnitude above the Km of ATP.
source: Furthermore, it would appear that an apo state, devoid of nucleotides, is unlikely to be populated or is transient under cellular ATP concentrations which are typically an order of magnitude above the Km of ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of cellular ATP concentrations and Km values.

claim: The 'alternating site hydrolysis' model posits that the two NBSs turnover ATP in an alternating manner constantly holding an intact ATP molecule in one of the NBSs.
source: The 'alternating site hydrolysis' model posits that the two NBSs turnover ATP in an alternating manner constantly holding an intact ATP molecule in one of the NBSs (Tombline and Senior, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The conjecture that the large inward-facing cavity observed in the apo structures is required to accommodate the large substrates of exporters has been challenged by the observation of smaller openings in the outward-facing conformations of MsbA and Sav1866.
source: The conjecture that the large inward-facing cavity observed in the apo structures is required to accommodate the large substrates of exporters has also been challenged (George and Jones, 2012) by the observation of smaller openings in the outward-facing conformations of MsbA and Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2006, 2007; Ward et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures and a review.

claim: A recent structure of an ABC heterodimer TM287/288 from the hyperthermophile Thermotoga maritima offered the first view of an ABC exporter in an inward-facing conformation where the two NBDs are partially engaged.
source: Further confounding the structural perspective, a recent structure of an ABC heterodimer TM287/288 from the hyperthermophile Thermotoga maritima offered the first view of an ABC exporter in an inward-facing conformation where the two NBDs are partially engaged (Hohl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a crystal structure.

claim: TM287/288 is a heterodimeric ABC transporter with non-canonical sequences in the Walker B and switch motifs of one subunit resulting in a catalytically impaired NBS.
source: Unlike MsbA, Sav1866 and Pgp, TM287/288 is a heterodimeric ABC transporter with non-canonical sequences in the Walker B and switch motifs of one subunit resulting in a catalytically impaired NBS.
evidence: This is a description of the TM287/288 structure and sequence features.

claim: In the TM287/288 structure, the impaired NBS is bridged by an AMP-PNP molecule while the intact NBS is more open creating an asymmetric NBD interface.
source: In the TM287/288 structure, the impaired NBS, also referred to as the degenerate NBS, is bridged by an AMP-PNP molecule while the intact NBS, referred to as the consensus NBS, is more open creating an asymmetric NBD interface.
evidence: This is a description of structural features from the TM287/288 crystal structure.

claim: Despite the partially engaged NBDs in TM287/288, the TMDs still form a chamber open to partitioning of substrates from the cytoplasm but does not appear to be accessible from the bilayer.
source: Despite the partially engaged NBDs, the TMDs still form a chamber open to partitioning of substrates from the cytoplasm but does not appear to be accessible from the bilayer (Hohl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the TM287/288 crystal structure.

claim: The TM287/288 structure is consistent with biochemical studies of bacterial ABC heterodimers that suggest catalytic asymmetry between the NBSs.
source: This structure is consistent with biochemical studies of bacterial ABC heterodimers (Lubelski et al., 2006; Zutz et al., 2011) that suggest catalytic asymmetry between the NBSs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: BmrCD from Bacillus subtilis is an ABC heterodimeric transporter with sequence modifications in the consensus motifs of the NBDs, including the replacement of the Walker B catalytic glutamate by an aspartate in BmrD.
source: Here, we have investigated the conformational changes associated with specific steps in the substrate-coupled ATPase cycle of an ABC heterodimeric transporter, BmrCD from Bacillus subtilis (Torres et al., 2009; Galián et al., 2011). Similar to other ABC heterodimers, sequence modifications in the consensus motifs of the NBDs, including the replacement of the Walker B catalytic glutamate by an aspartate in BmrD, suggest that ATP turnover is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and is a description of BmrCD sequence features.

claim: BmrC and BmrD genes are upregulated in the response of B. subtilis to antibiotics exposure.
source: BmrC and BmrD genes are upregulated in the response of B. subtilis to antibiotics exposure and BmrCD confers multidrug transport activity on inside-out Escherichia coli membrane vesicles (Torres et al., 2009) and in reconstituted giant unilamellar vesicles (Dezi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BmrCD confers multidrug transport activity on inside-out Escherichia coli membrane vesicles and in reconstituted giant unilamellar vesicles.
source: BmrC and BmrD genes are upregulated in the response of B. subtilis to antibiotics exposure and BmrCD confers multidrug transport activity on inside-out Escherichia coli membrane vesicles (Torres et al., 2009) and in reconstituted giant unilamellar vesicles (Dezi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A homology model of BmrCD was built using the crystal structure of AMP-PNP-bound TM287/288 as a template.
source: To guide in the selection of residues for spin labeling, a homology model of BmrCD was built using the crystal structure of AMP-PNP-bound TM287/288 (Hohl et al., 2012) as a template (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Cysteine-free and spin-labeled BmrCD mutants hydrolyze ATP in dodecyl maltoside (DDM) micelles and in lipid bilayers.
source: We verified that cysteine-free and spin-labeled BmrCD mutants hydrolyze ATP in dodecyl maltoside (DDM) micelles and in lipid bilayers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The rates of ATP turnover are stimulated by the transport substrate Hoechst33342 except for the 533/625 pair.
source: Importanly, the rates of ATP turnover are stimulated by the transport substrate Hoechst33342 (hereafter referred as Hoechst) except for the 533/625 pair.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of nucleotide or substrates (apo state), BmrCD NBDs are disengaged as evident from distances between spin labels that are larger than those predicted on the basis of the nucleotide-bound TM287/288 crystal structure and the BmrCD homology model.
source: In the absence of nucleotide or substrates, hereafter referred to as the apo state, BmrCD NBDs are disengaged as evident from distances between spin labels that are larger than those predicted on the basis of the nucleotide-bound TM287/288 crystal structure and the BmrCD homology model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data and comparison to structural models.

claim: Featureless DEER decays at spin label pairs 533/625 and 555/647 reflect distances longer than 50 and 70 Å, respectively, in the apo state.
source: Featureless DEER decays at spin label pairs 533/625 and 555/647, which were designed to monitor the NBD dimer interface, firmly reflect distances longer than 50 and 70 Å, respectively (black trace, Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The average distance and broad distribution at 533/625 in BmrCD are similar to those observed at the equivalent MsbA site 539.
source: The average distance and broad distribution at 533/625 are similar to those observed at the equivalent MsbA site 539 (Borbat et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data on MsbA.

claim: The distances at 533/625 and 555/647 in the apo state report a relatively large separation between the NBDs similar to that of inward-open apo MsbA and are suggestive of considerable conformational flexibility.
source: Accordingly, they report a relatively large separation between the NBDs in the apo state similar to that of inward-open apo MsbA (Borbat et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2009) and are suggestive of considerable conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in comparison to previous MsbA studies.

claim: ATP turnover followed by Vanadate (Vi) trapping stabilizes the transporter in an otherwise high-energy post-hydrolysis state (HES), also referred to as the transition state of ATP hydrolysis.
source: ATP turnover followed by Vanadate (Vi) trapping stabilizes the transporter in an otherwise high-energy post-hydrolysis state (HES), also referred to as the transition state of ATP hydrolysis (Sharma and Davidson, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study describing the Vi trapping method.

claim: The energy input from ATP hydrolysis leads to a large relative movement that brings the two NBDs closer together as manifested by the reduction in the average distances at 533/625 and 555/647 to about 25 and 45 Å, respectively, in the HES state.
source: The energy input from ATP hydrolysis leads to a large relative movement that brings the two NBDs closer together as manifested by the reduction in the average distances at 533/625 and 555/647 to about 25 and 45 Å, respectively (red trace, Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The narrower distance distributions in the HES state indicate a restriction of NBD conformational flexibility.
source: The narrower distance distributions indicate a restriction of NBD conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER distance distribution data.

claim: The distance distributions in the HES state are consistent with the formation of a closed NBD sandwich similar to that observed in the AMP-PNP bound crystal structures of MsbA and Sav1866.
source: Compared to the equivalent sites in MsbA (Borbat et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2009) (539, 561), these distance distributions are consistent with the formation of a closed NBD sandwich similar to that observed in the AMP-PNP bound crystal structures of MsbA (Ward et al., 2007) and Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in comparison to crystal structures and previous MsbA studies.

claim: Binding of the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP stabilizes a conformation distinct from that observed under trapped or apo conditions.
source: Binding of the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP stabilizes a conformation distinct from that observed under trapped or apo conditions (blue trace, Figure 1C) and well outside the range predicted by the crystal structure and the homology model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In MsbA, ATP binding and HES trapping stabilize the same conformation of the NBD dimer.
source: This is in stark contrast to the ABC homodimer, MsbA, where ATP binding and HES trapping stabilize the same conformation of the NBD dimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data on MsbA shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The 555/647 pair suggests an arrangement of the NBDs where the spin labels are separated by a longer average distance than in the HES but not as disengaged as apo in the AMP-PNP bound state.
source: The 555/647 pair suggests an arrangement of the NBDs where the spin labels are separated by a longer average distance than in the HES but not as disengaged as apo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATP binding, mimicked by AMP-PNP, nucleates the formation of an NBD dimer distinct from the canonical closed NBD sandwich observed in the crystal structures of nucleotide-bound MsbA and Sav1866.
source: These characteristics suggest that ATP binding, mimicked by AMP-PNP, nucleates the formation of an NBD dimer distinct from the canonical closed NBD sandwich observed in the crystal structures of nucleotide-bound MsbA (Ward et al., 2007) and Sav1866 (Dawson and Locher, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in comparison to crystal structures.

claim: A similar distance to the AMP-PNP bound state is observed in the presence of ADP, suggesting that both nucleotides stabilize an intermediate state of the NBD dimer.
source: Remarkably, a similar distance is observed in the presence of ADP (Figure 1C) suggesting that both nucleotides stabilize this intermediate state of the NBD dimer.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Spin labels reporting on the consensus NBS have overlapping distributions in the AMP-PNP-bound and trapped HES intermediates.
source: Consistently, spin labels reporting on the consensus NBS have overlapping distributions in the AMP-PNP-bound and trapped HES intermediates whereas at the degenerate site the distributions are by and large distinct (Figure 2, compare panels A, B, and C with D, E, and F).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the degenerate NBS, the distributions in the AMP-PNP-bound and trapped HES intermediates are by and large distinct.
source: Consistently, spin labels reporting on the consensus NBS have overlapping distributions in the AMP-PNP-bound and trapped HES intermediates whereas at the degenerate site the distributions are by and large distinct (Figure 2, compare panels A, B, and C with D, E, and F).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The breadth of the AMP-PNP distribution at the consensus NBS demonstrates that ATP binding enables a range of conformations to be populated that includes the HES.
source: The breadth of the AMP-PNP distribution at the consensus NBS demonstrates that ATP binding enables a range of conformations to be populated that includes the HES.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required to observe an HES population at the degenerate NBS as inferred from the predominantly distinct distributions in the presence of AMP-PNP and ADP-Vi.
source: In contrast, ATP hydrolysis is required to observe an HES population at the degenerate NBS as inferred from the predominantly distinct distributions in the presence of AMP-PNP and ADP-Vi.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the presence of excess ADP, the degenerate NBS has a predominantly ATP-bound like conformation while the consensus NBS has a significant population of apo-like conformation.
source: In the presence of excess ADP, the degenerate NBS has a predominantly ATP-bound like conformation while the consensus NBS has a significant population of apo-like conformation (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both NBSs disengage in the absence of nucleotides consistent with the relative distance and conformational flexibility observed at the NBD interface.
source: Both NBSs disengage in the absence of nucleotides consistent with the relative distance and conformational flexibility observed at the NBD interface (Figure 2, black traces).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Addition of the transport substrate Hoechst did not change the distance distributions of the AMP-PNP and ADP-Vi states.
source: Addition of the transport substrate Hoechst (Torres et al., 2009) did not change the distance distributions of the AMP-PNP and ADP-Vi states (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pattern of average distances observed in the apo state of BmrCD is consistent with an open intracellular side and a relatively more closed extracellular side.
source: The pattern of average distances observed in the apo state of BmrCD is consistent with an open intracellular side and a relatively more closed extracellular side (Figure 3B,C, black trace, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The intracellular side of apo BmrCD appears to be more closed than that of apo MsbA consistent with TM287/288 structure and the homology model.
source: Furthermore, the intracellular side of apo BmrCD appears to be more closed than that of apo MsbA consistent with TM287/288 structure and the homology model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in comparison to MsbA and structural models.

claim: The distance between the symmetry-related residues 103 in the MsbA homodimer is outside the range of measurable distances by DEER, at least 10 Å longer than the distance measured at the equivalent BmrCD pair, 96/188.
source: For instance, the distance between the symmetry-related residues 103 in the MsbA homodimer (previous work Borbat et al., 2007 and see below) is outside the range of measurable distances by DEER, at least 10 Å longer than the distance measured at the equivalent BmrCD pair, 96/188.
evidence: This is a comparison of DEER data between BmrCD and MsbA.

claim: While ATP binding, mimicked by addition of AMP-PNP, induces the formation of a distinct NBD intermediate in BmrCD, this conformational change is not propagated to the TMD.
source: While ATP binding, mimicked by addition of AMP-PNP, induces the formation of a distinct NBD intermediate in BmrCD, we found that this conformational change is not propagated to the TMD.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spin label pairs at the intracellular and extracellular sides have identical distance distributions in apo and AMP-PNP-bound states.
source: Spin label pairs at the intracellular and extracellular sides have identical distance distributions in apo and AMP-PNP-bound (Figure 3, black and blue traces respectively).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The finding that TMD distance distributions are identical in apo and AMP-PNP-bound states suggests relative flexibility between the NBD and TMD that allows large independent movement of the former upon ATP binding.
source: This finding suggests relative flexibility between the NBD and TMD that allows large independent movement of the former upon ATP binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data.

claim: When ATP is hydrolyzed and ADP subsequently trapped by the addition of Vi, concomitant shifts in the average distance at the intra- and extracellular sides of the transporter are observed.
source: In contrast, when ATP is hydrolyzed and ADP subsequently trapped by the addition of Vi, we observed concomitant shifts in the average distance at the intra- and extracellular sides of the transporter.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Coupled to the formation of the NBD closed dimer, ATP hydrolysis induces closing of the intracellular side and opening of the extracellular side consistent with an alternating access mechanism involving inward-facing and outward-facing conformations.
source: Coupled to the formation of the NBD closed dimer, ATP hydrolysis induces closing of the intracellular side and opening of the extracellular side consistent with an alternating access mechanism involving inward-facing and outward-facing conformations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in the context of the alternating access model.

claim: Compared to MsbA (residue 103), the distance change at the intracellular side is of smaller magnitude (approximately 15 Å for BmrCD 96/188 vs 25 Å for MsbA 103) primarily due to a closer distance between the TMDs in the apo conformation of BmrCD.
source: Compared to MsbA (residue 103) (Borbat et al., 2007) the distance change at the intracellular side is of smaller magnitude (approximately 15 Å for BmrCD 96/188 vs 25 Å for MsbA 103) primarily due to a closer distance between the TMDs in the apo conformation of BmrCD (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of DEER data between BmrCD and MsbA.

claim: While conformational changes in MsbA are induced by the binding of AMP-PNP, the inward- to outward-facing transition in BmrCD requires ATP hydrolysis revealing a distinct power stroke between homodimers and heterodimers.
source: More importantly, while conformational changes in MsbA are induced by the binding of AMP-PNP, the inward- to outward-facing transition in BmrCD requires ATP hydrolysis revealing a distinct power stroke between homodimers and heterodimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of DEER data between BmrCD and MsbA.

claim: Reconstitution in nanodiscs stimulated the ATP turnover rates of BmrCD-WT and BmrCD-WT* by 11–14-fold relative to detergent micelles.
source: Reconstitution in nanodiscs stimulated the ATP turnover rates of BmrCD-WT and BmrCD-WT* by 11–14-fold relative to detergent micelles (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rates of ATP turnover in nanodiscs were further stimulated two-fold in the presence of Hoechst.
source: The rates were further stimulated two-fold in the presence of Hoechst.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Distance distributions in nanodiscs reveal components almost identical to those in detergent micelles.
source: Distance distributions in nanodiscs reveal components almost identical to those in detergent micelles (Compare Figure 4 with Figures 1–3,).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 4 compared to Figures 1-3.

claim: Spin label pairs in the NBD show distinct distances in the apo state, AMP-PNP bound state, and the HES consistent with three conformations of the NBDs in nanodiscs.
source: Spin label pairs in the NBD show distinct distances in the apo state, AMP-PNP bound state, and the HES consistent with three conformations of the NBDs (Figure 4, top panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Distance distributions of spin label pairs in the TMD identify only two conformational states corresponding to inward and outward-facing conformations in nanodiscs.
source: In contrast, distance distributions of spin label pairs in the TMD identify only two conformational states corresponding to inward and outward-facing conformations (Figure 4, lower panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required to transition between inward and outward-facing states in nanodiscs, whereas BmrCD bound to AMP-PNP is in the inward-facing conformation.
source: ATP hydrolysis is required to transition between these states whereas BmrCD bound to AMP-PNP- is in the inward-facing conformation, in agreement with the observations in detergent micelles described above (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 4 and comparison to Figure 3.

claim: There is a correspondence between conformational states in detergent micelles and lipid bilayers and the power stroke is essentially identical.
source: Thus, not only is there a correspondence between conformational states in detergent micelles and lipid bilayers but also the power stroke is essentially identical.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of DEER data in detergent and nanodiscs.

claim: The transition between inward- and outward-facing conformations in nanodiscs shows a more stringent dependence on the presence of substrate.
source: Remarkably, the transition between inward- and outward-facing conformations in nanodiscs shows a more stringent dependence on the presence of substrate (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Although ATP is turned over in the absence of substrate, transmission of this hydrolysis step is enhanced by the presence of the substrate Hoechst.
source: Thus, although ATP is turned over in the absence of substrate, transmission of this hydrolysis step is enhanced by the presence of the substrate Hoechst.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in nanodiscs.

claim: At the degenerate NBS, predominantly two-component distance distributions are observed under turnover conditions that reflect two distinct transporter populations.
source: At the degenerate NBS, we observed predominantly two-component distance distributions that reflect two distinct transporter populations (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: By comparing distance distributions for the same spin label pair in trapped intermediates and under turnover conditions, the two components at the degenerate NBS are identified as arising from nucleotide-bound (ATP or ADP) and HES-like states.
source: By comparing distance distributions for the same spin label pair in trapped intermediates and under turnover conditions, the two components are identified as arising from nucleotide-bound (ATP or ADP) and HES-like states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data by comparison to trapped states.

claim: The population ratio of the two components at the degenerate NBS shifts from the HES-like towards the nucleotide-bound state with little if any apo population observed at the two time points.
source: The population ratio of the two components shifts from the HES-like towards the nucleotide-bound state with little if any apo population observed at the two time points.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Multicomponent distributions at the consensus NBS show, in addition to the HES-like and nucleotide-bound states, clear evidence of an apo-like population where the two NBDs are locally disengaged.
source: In contrast, multicomponent distributions at the consensus NBS (Figure 5B) show, in addition to the HES-like and nucleotide-bound states, clear evidence of an apo-like population where the two NBDs are locally disengaged.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The two NBSs cycle between conformational states as ATP is bound, hydrolyzed and Pi and ADP are released.
source: Thus, the two NBSs cycle between conformational states as ATP is bound, hydrolyzed and Pi and ADP are released.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: The differences in the population amplitude of states at the two NBSs reveal that the two NBSs do not have to concurrently be in the same catalytic intermediate.
source: However, the differences in the population amplitude of these states reveal that the two NBSs do not have to concurrently be in the same catalytic intermediate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: The distributions under turnover conditions imply the existence of a transporter intermediate wherein the degenerate NBS is ATP-bound while the consensus NBS assumes an apo-like conformation.
source: Therefore, the distributions under turnover conditions imply the existence of a transporter intermediate wherein the degenerate NBS is ATP-bound while the consensus NBS assumes an apo-like conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: The distributions under turnover conditions imply the presence of another state of the transporter wherein the degenerate NBS is in a HES-like state and the consensus NBS is in the ATP-bound conformation.
source: Similarly, we can infer the presence of another state of the transporter wherein the degenerate NBS is in a HES-like state and the consensus NBS is in the ATP-bound conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: Longer incubation times shift the distribution towards the ATP/ADP-bound population at the degenerate NBS.
source: Longer incubation times shift the distribution towards the ATP/ADP-bound population at the degenerate NBS (compare 1 and 5 min time points in Figure 5C) while at similar incubation times, the consensus site shows a considerably larger population in the ATP-bound and the apo states (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The addition of the substrate Hoechst, which accelerates the rate of ATP hydrolysis, shifts the populations at both NBSs towards those obtained at the longer incubation time.
source: The addition of the substrate Hoechst, which accelerates the rate of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), simply shifts the populations at both NBSs towards those obtained at the longer incubation time.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 5 and ATPase data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The substrate-coupled ATP turnover cycle of BmrCD involves the same conformational states sampled in the absence of substrate.
source: Thus, the substrate-coupled ATP turnover cycle of BmrCD involves the same conformational states sampled in the absence of substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DEER data under turnover conditions with and without substrate.

claim: Coupled to the ATP hydrolysis cycle of the NBSs, the TMD undergoes an inward- to outward-facing transition as evidenced by the time dependence of the distance distributions.
source: Coupled to the ATP hydrolysis cycle of the NBSs, the TMD undergoes an inward- to outward-facing transition as evidenced by the time dependence of the distance distributions (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The TMDs show multi-component distance distributions under turnover conditions.
source: Similar to the NBSs, the TMDs show multi-component distance distributions.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The equilibrium favors the inward-facing conformation of the TMD as demonstrated by the ratio of the two populations at high ATP concentrations.
source: However, the equilibrium favors the inward-facing conformation as demonstrated by the ratio of the two populations at high ATP concentrations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The predominance of the inward-facing conformation of the TMD presumably reflects the failure of ATP binding to switch TMD accessibility from inward-facing to outward-facing.
source: This presumably reflects the failure of ATP binding to switch TMD accessibility from inward-facing to outward-facing (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data in the context of previous findings.

claim: The major novel finding of this paper is that sequence asymmetry in the NBDs shapes the mechanism of energy transduction in ABC exporters.
source: The major novel finding of this paper is that sequence asymmetry in the NBDs shapes the mechanism of energy transduction in ABC exporters.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Modifications of the Walker B, signature and/or switch motifs sequences, which lead to selective catalytic impairment of one of the NBSs in a subclass of ABC exporters, are associated with fundamental differences in the conformational dynamics of the NBDs and in the power stroke of transport.
source: Modifications of the Walker B, signature and/or switch motifs sequences, which lead to selective catalytic impairment of one of the NBSs in a subclass of ABC exporters (Gao et al., 2000; Aleksandrov et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2006; Procko et al., 2009; Boncoeur et al., 2012), are associated with fundamental differences in the conformational dynamics of the NBDs and in the power stroke of transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In contrast to the ATP-induced association/dissociation cycle of NBDs in bacterial homodimers, the NBDs of heterodimers form structurally asymmetric dimers as a consequence of ATP binding and its subsequent hydrolysis.
source: In contrast to the ATP-induced association/dissociation cycle of NBDs in bacterial homodimers reported previously (Borbat et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2009) and further confirmed here, the NBDs of heterodimers form structurally asymmetric dimers as a consequence of ATP binding and its subsequent hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of BmrCD and MsbA data.

claim: Conformations were uncovered wherein the impaired NBS holds on to an ATP molecule while the consensus NBS disengages enabling product release and rebinding of ATP.
source: We uncovered conformations wherein the impaired NBS holds on to an ATP molecule while the consensus NBS disengages enabling product release and rebinding of ATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: Asymmetric NBD conformations were hypothesized from the elegant mechanistic analysis of Pgp by Senior et al. but were not directly detected.
source: Asymmetric NBD conformations were hypothesized from the elegant mechanistic analysis of Pgp by Senior et al. but were not directly detected (Tombline and Senior, 2005; Tombline et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Pgp.

claim: The distinct mechanism of heterodimers requires a less efficient coupling between the NBD and TMD, a 'conformational leak', to enable NBD movement without transmission to the TMDs.
source: We propose that the distinct mechanism of heterodimers requires a less efficient coupling between the NBD and TMD, a 'conformational leak', to enable NBD movement without transmission to the TMDs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: The less efficient coupling between NBD and TMD would require a tuning of the sequences and interactions of the IH1 and IH2 coupling loops and possibly the cytoplasmic extension of TMs, regions hypothesized to form the transmission interface between the NBDs and TMDs of ABC transporters.
source: This would require a tuning of the sequences and interactions of the IH1 and IH2 coupling loops and possibly the cytoplasmic extension of TMs, regions hypothesized to form the transmission interface between the NBDs and TMDs of ABC transporters (Hollenstein et al., 2007; Oancea et al., 2009; Loo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a substantial impact of lipids on the coupling between the NBD and TMD.
source: There is a substantial impact of lipids on the coupling between the NBD and TMD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of data in detergent and nanodiscs.

claim: Transmission of the conformational changes to the TMD is more stringently dependent on the presence of substrate in lipid bilayers.
source: Transmission of the conformational changes to the TMD is more stringently dependent on the presence of substrate in lipid bilyaers.
evidence: This is supported by DEER data in nanodiscs shown in Figure 4.

claim: This finding is consistent with previous work revealing that lipids can shift the conformational preferences of ion-coupled transporters.
source: This finding is consistent with previous work revealing that lipids can shift the conformational preferences of ion-coupled transporters (Hanelt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: NBS distance distributions capture the interconversion of the transporter between conformations corresponding to those observed under trapped conditions, thereby establishing the direct relevance of the trapped conformations to the substrate-coupled ATPase cycle.
source: NBS distance distributions capture the interconversion of the transporter between conformations corresponding to those observed under trapped conditions, thereby establishing the direct relevance of the trapped conformations to the substrate-coupled ATPase cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: The observation of a steady state population of apo-like conformation of the consensus NBS, even in the presence of excess ATP, prompts the conclusion that disengagement of this NBS is required for ADP-Pi dissociation and subsequent binding of ATP.
source: Furthermore, the observation of a steady state population of apo-like conformation of the consensus NBS, even in the presence of excess ATP, prompts us to conclude that disengagement of this NBS is required for ADP-Pi dissociation and subsequent binding of ATP, thereby establishing the mechanistic significance of a local apo-like conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: In the presence of cellular ATP concentrations, BmrCD will have at least one ATP molecule bound, most likely at the degenerate NBS as evidenced by the fact that an apo-like conformation was nearly undetectable at this NBS in the presence of excess ATP.
source: In the presence of cellular ATP concentrations, BmrCD will have at least one ATP molecule bound, most likely at the degenerate NBS as evidenced by the fact that an apo-like conformation was nearly undetectable at this NBS in the presence of excess ATP.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: An ATP-bound resting state does not hinder substrate access to the putative binding chamber at the TMD interface, since ATP binding does not induce closure of the cytoplasmic side of BmrCD.
source: Such an ATP-bound resting state does not hinder substrate access to the putative binding chamber at the TMD interface, since ATP binding does not induce closure of the cytoplasmic side of BmrCD.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data showing no TMD conformational change upon ATP binding.

claim: ATP binding to the consensus NBS yields an intermediate with two ATP molecules bound, referred to as a pre-hydrolysis intermediate reminiscent of the pre-hydrolysis complex observed in a crystal structure of the maltose transporter, MalK.
source: ATP binding to the consensus NBS yields an intermediate with two ATP molecules bound ('1' in Figure 8A). We refer to this conformation of the NBD dimer (Figure 2) as a pre-hydrolysis intermediate reminiscent of the pre-hydrolysis complex observed in a crystal structure of the maltose transporter, MalK (Oldham and Chen, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in comparison to a crystal structure.

claim: In the pre-hydrolysis intermediate, the NBDs are engaged but the NBSs have not formed the canonical configuration and are therefore not catalytically competent.
source: In this conformation, the NBDs are engaged but the NBSs have not formed the canonical configuration and are therefore not catalytically competent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data.

claim: ATP turnover is initiated by fluctuations at the consensus NBS which enables transition to a hydrolysis-competent configuration (HES-like) as deduced from the overlapping distance distributions.
source: ATP turnover is initiated by fluctuations at the consensus NBS which enables transition to a hydrolysis-competent configuration (HES-like) as deduced from the overlapping distance distributions in Figure 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The hydrolysis-competent configuration is a relatively minor population of the transporter which likely explains the relatively slow ATP turnover by BmrCD.
source: This is a relatively minor population of the transporter which likely explains the relatively slow ATP turnover by BmrCD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data and ATPase activity data.

claim: ATP hydrolysis switches TMD accessibility thereby catalyzing the extrusion of the substrate.
source: ATP hydrolysis switches TMD accessibility thereby catalyzing the extrusion of the substrate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data showing TMD conformational change upon ATP hydrolysis.

claim: Turnover rates are stimulated if the substrate binds prior to hydrolysis but there is a considerable basal consumption of ATP.
source: Turnover rates are stimulated if the substrate binds prior to hydrolysis but there is a considerable basal consumption of ATP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: While there is evidence of ATP turnover by impaired NBSs, consideration of the reaction mechanism as well as previous biochemical studies of ABC heterodimers support an intrinsically slower rate at the degenerate NBS.
source: While there is evidence of ATP turnover by impaired NBSs, consideration of the reaction mechanism as well as previous biochemical studies of ABC heterodimers support an intrinsically slower rate at the degenerate NBS (Procko et al., 2006; Zutz et al., 2011; Boncoeur et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: ADP and Pi are released from the consensus site prior to hydrolysis at the degenerate site enabling multiple rounds of asymmetric ATP hydrolysis without the complete disengagement of the NBDs to an apo conformation.
source: Therefore, ADP and Pi are released from the consensus site prior to hydrolysis at the degenerate site enabling multiple rounds of asymmetric ATP hydrolysis without the complete disengagement of the NBDs to an apo conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: Slow ATP hydrolysis at the degenerate NBS would require release of ADP and Pi and rebinding of ATP most likely through the population of a local apo-like conformation.
source: Slow ATP hydrolysis at the degenerate NBS would require release of ADP and Pi and rebinding of ATP most likely through the population of a local apo-like conformation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: The negligible population of apo-like degenerate NBS and the fact that ADP-bound NBDs form a partially engaged dimer argue against significant population of an apo state of the transporter where the two NBDs are separated by more than 50 Å.
source: However, the negligible population of apo-like degenerate NBS and the fact that ADP-bound NBDs form a partially engaged dimer argue against significant population of an apo state of the transporter where the two NBDs are separated by more than 50 Å.
evidence: This is an inference from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: The 'global' apo state (as in Figure 1) appears not to be mechanistically relevant in the ATP hydrolysis cycle of ABC heterodimers.
source: Thus, this 'global' apo state (as in Figure 1) appears not to be mechanistically relevant in the ATP hydrolysis cycle of ABC heterodimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DEER data under turnover conditions.

claim: ADP-Pi release, as a consequence of infrequent hydrolysis at the degenerate site, occurs while ATP is bound at the consensus NBS.
source: We propose that ADP-Pi release, as a consequence of infrequent hydrolysis at the degenerate site, occurs while ATP is bound at the consensus NBS.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: Hydrolysis at the consensus NBS requires transition of the degenerate NBS to an ATP-occluded state along the lines of the model proposed for Pgp on the basis of experiments with catalytically impaired NBSs.
source: We speculate that hydrolysis at the consensus NBS requires transition of the degenerate NBS to an ATP-occluded state along the lines of the model proposed for Pgp on the basis of experiments with catalytically impaired NBSs (Tombline and Senior, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ATP-occluded state at the degenerate NBS would relax to the nucleotide-bound conformation following hydrolysis at the consensus NBS.
source: This state would relax to the nucleotide-bound conformation following hydrolysis at the consensus NBS (state 3 in Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: For ABC homodimers, the NBSs are identical in sequence and there is no experimental evidence of catalytic inequivalence.
source: For the latter, the NBSs are identical in sequence and there is no experimental evidence of catalytic inequivalence.
evidence: This is a statement about ABC homodimers based on knowledge and the MsbA data.

claim: Analysis of MsbA conformational dynamics is entirely consistent with a model of turnover that invokes engaged and disengaged NBD states, symmetric NBS conformations, and tight structural coupling between the NBDs and the TMDs.
source: Analysis of MsbA conformational dynamics reported previously (Dong et al., 2005; Borbat et al., 2007; Zou and Mchaourab, 2009) and extended here is entirely consistent with a model of turnover that invokes engaged and disengaged NBD states, symmetric NBS conformations, and tight structural coupling between the NBDs and the TMDs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MsbA data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The controversy regarding NBD disengagement vs constant contact is a consequence of extrapolation of models between mechanistically distinct classes of ABC exporters.
source: We conclude from the comparative analysis of BmrCD and MsbA conformational cycles that the controversy regarding NBD disengagement vs constant contact (George and Jones, 2012) is a consequence of extrapolation of models between mechanistically distinct classes of ABC exporters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of BmrCD and MsbA.

claim: The structural mechanism of ABC heterodimers described here is a remarkable example of variations on a common conformational cycle in the context of conserved transporter architecture.
source: The structural mechanism of ABC heterodimers described here is a remarkable example of variations on a common conformational cycle in the context of conserved transporter architecture.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: While all ABC transporters derive energy from an ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle, fundamental differences exist in the regulation of ATP turnover by catalytic elements and/or structural intermediates as evidenced here.
source: While all ABC transporters derive energy from an ATP binding and hydrolysis cycle, fundamental differences exist in the regulation of ATP turnover by catalytic elements and/or structural intermediates as evidenced here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: Although it was anticipated that the inward- to outward-facing transition of ABC exporters would follow the structural mechanics defined by the structures of MsbA, coupling of the TMD transition to the ATPase cycle is not identical between subclasses of exporters.
source: Although it was anticipated that the inward- to outward-facing transition of ABC exporters would follow the structural mechanics defined by the structures of MsbA (Ward et al., 2007), we show in this work that coupling of the TMD transition to the ATPase cycle is not identical between subclasses of exporters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of BmrCD and MsbA data.

claim: Evidence of more variation in the coupling mechanism has emerged recently from a structure of a human ABC homodimer where the NBSs are disengaged even in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: Evidence of more variation in the coupling mechanism has emerged recently from a structure of a human ABC homodimer where the NBSs are disengaged even in the presence of AMP-PNP (Shintre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent crystal structure.

claim: If TMD conformational changes require hydrolysis of a single ATP molecule in heterodimers, it raises the conundrum of why two molecules are hydrolyzed in ABC homodimers to achieve what would appear to be similar type of mechanical work.
source: Finally, if indeed TMD conformational changes require hydrolysis of a single ATP molecule in heterodimers, it raises the conundrum of why two molecules are hydrolyzed in ABC homodimers to achieve what would appear to be similar type of mechanical work.
evidence: This is a question raised based on the findings of the study.

claim: A homology model of the inward-facing BmrCD was constructed with MODELLER, using the crystal structure of the asymmetric ABC transporter TM287/288 (PDB: 3QF4) as the template.
source: A homology model of the inward-facing BmrCD was constructed with MODELLER (Marti-Renom et al., 2000), using the crystal structure of the asymmetric ABC transporter TM287/288 (PDB: 3QF4) (Hohl et al., 2012) as the template.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: TMD287 was chosen as the template for BmrC and TMD288 as a template for BmrD in order to correctly map the consensus and degenerate nucleotide-binding sites.
source: In order to correctly map the consensus and degenerate nucleotide-binding sites, TMD287 was chosen as the template for BmrC and TMD288 as a template for BmrD.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Substitution of the native cysteines with alanines marginally reduces the Vmax of ATP turnover.
source: Substitution of the native cysteines with alanines marginally reduces the Vmax of ATP turnover.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: All spin-labeled BmrCD pairs used for this study turnover ATP well above the background observed from inhibition by vanadate.
source: All spin-labeled BmrCD pairs used for this study turnover ATP well above the background observed from inhibition by vanadate.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Vmax increased for all pairs following the addition of Hoechst although the level of stimulation was somewhat variable.
source: Vmax increased for all pairs following the addition of Hoechst although the level of stimulation was somewhat variable.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Hoechst33342 does not stimulate the ATPase activity of cysteine-less MsbA (MsbA-WT*).
source: Hoechst33342 (hereafter referred to as Hoechst) does not stimulate, but vanadate inhibits the ATPase activity of cysteine-less MsbA (MsbA-WT*) and (B) spin label mutants.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vanadate inhibits the ATPase activity of cysteine-less MsbA (MsbA-WT*) and spin label mutants.
source: Hoechst33342 (hereafter referred to as Hoechst) does not stimulate, but vanadate inhibits the ATPase activity of cysteine-less MsbA (MsbA-WT*) and (B) spin label mutants.
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of ATP induces the formation of the closed NBD dimer and concomitantly drives the transition to an outward-facing conformation of the TMD in MsbA.
source: Binding of ATP induces the formation of the closed NBD dimer and concomitantly drives the transition to an outward-facing conformation of the TMD (C and D)
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of excess ATP, the equilibrium favors the outward-facing conformation in MsbA.
source: In the presence of excess ATP, the equilibrium favors the outward-facing conformation (green trace).
evidence: This is supported by DEER data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The predominance of the outward-facing conformation of the TMD in MsbA is consistent with the persistence of the NBS short distance component under turnover conditions.
source: The predominance of the outward-facing conformation of the TMD is consistent with the persistence of the NBS short distance component under turnover conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DEER data shown in Figure 7.
